forces.title: Strong infrastructure investment supports specialized construction demand.
forces.description: Infrastructure investment, backed by EU funds and spending on energy and digital networks, is a primary driver for the broader construction sector. This includes civil engineering projects, such as water and wastewater treatment plants and related environmental engineering works. Additionally, a focus on renovation and sustainability projects within specialized construction segments further boosts demand for modern and efficient water and waste management solutions, offsetting weaknesses in other construction areas.
forces.source_title: Europe's construction sector faces a period of weak growth

forces.title: High financing costs hinder new construction projects and buyer affordability.
forces.description: Higher interest rates make financing new construction projects more expensive for governments, industrial clients, and developers. This increased financing cost translates into reduced investment appetite and can lead to the postponement or cancellation of new projects, directly impacting the demand for EPC contracts in water, waste, and environmental engineering. The challenge of absorbing further cost increases due to rising interest rates caps overall sector momentum.
forces.source_title: Europe's construction sector faces a period of weak growth

forces.title: Rising energy prices increase material costs and squeeze profit margins.
forces.description: Higher energy prices are pushing up production costs for energy-intensive materials crucial for construction, such as concrete, cement, and bricks. While material prices are generally rising gradually, the increased input costs are harder for contractors to pass through the value chain due to clients facing their own financial constraints. This dynamic puts significant pressure on profit margins for water, waste, and environmental engineering EPC firms, increasing the risk of disputes and project delays.
forces.source_title: Europe's construction sector faces a period of weak growth

forces.title: Supply chain disruptions from low water levels and geopolitical tensions.
forces.description: Low water levels in inland waterways are hindering the transport of raw materials like sand, gravel, and chemicals, leading to increased transport costs and delayed deliveries in the construction supply chain. This compounds with geopolitical risks, such as the Middle East conflict, which trigger high energy inflation and widespread supply chain disruptions, impacting the availability and cost of industrial raw materials and chemicals. These disruptions can significantly affect project timelines and costs for water, waste, and environmental engineering projects.
forces.source_title: Europe's construction sector faces a period of weak growth

forces.title: Slowing Dutch infrastructure growth due to staff shortages and nitrogen restrictions.
forces.description: The strong growth previously seen in the Dutch infrastructure sector is decelerating significantly. Key impediments include persistent staff shortages, which constrain project execution capacity, and nitrogen restrictions, which impose environmental limitations on new developments. Additionally, limited government budgets lead to a prioritization of maintenance over new construction, reducing the pipeline for large-scale EPC projects in water and environmental engineering despite existing high production levels.

forces.title: Cost inflation and staff shortages threaten Irish construction sector's recovery.
forces.description: Despite a strengthening construction sector in Ireland, particularly in civil engineering, significant risks remain from ongoing cost inflation for materials and labor. Furthermore, staff shortages and lengthening delivery times exacerbate these cost pressures and complicate project execution. Water, waste, and environmental engineering firms need to build flexibility into contracts, stress-test project margins, and manage supply chain partners closely to mitigate these risks and ensure the profitability and timely completion of projects amidst an otherwise positive demand environment.

forces.title: Energy supply and data center buildout boost Norwegian engineering prospects.
forces.description: While overall construction activity in Norway is subdued, specialized areas like energy supply development and new data center buildouts are lifting prospects for related engineering services. Data centers require significant water and waste management infrastructure, and energy supply projects often entail environmental engineering aspects for permitting and compliance. This focus on critical infrastructure and industrial expansion provides a concentrated source of demand for EPC contractors in water, waste, and environmental engineering, offsetting the broader weakness in residential and commercial new builds.
forces.source_title: Regional Network report 1/2026: Minor changes in growth prospects

forces.title: Increased rehabilitation and maintenance activity offsets new construction slowdown.
forces.description: In Norway, despite low activity in new-build construction, there's a discernible pickup in rehabilitation and maintenance projects for both private and public-sector entities. This shift towards upgrading existing infrastructure rather than constructing new facilities creates demand for environmental engineering services focused on modernizing, improving efficiency, and ensuring compliance for older water and waste treatment plants. This trend provides a more stable, albeit potentially lower-value, project pipeline for the sector.
forces.source_title: Regional Network report 1/2026: Minor changes in growth prospects

forces.title: Weak profitability persists in Norwegian construction despite some activity improvements.
forces.description: Despite some improvement in activity due to specialized projects and cost control, overall profitability in the Norwegian construction sector remains weak. High construction costs for new homes, commercial, and public buildings lead to project postponements. This pressure on margins, coupled with global turbulence, cost growth, and higher interest rates, prompts many contacts to delay or halt investment projects. This directly affects EPC firms in water, waste, and environmental engineering by making new contracts less attractive or harder to secure with viable margins.
forces.source_title: Regional Network report 2/2026: Recruitment difficulties have eased somewhat

forces.title: Overall subdued EU construction sector growth caps momentum for specialized engineering.
forces.description: The EU construction output is expected to grow by a marginal 0.5% in 2026, following a decline in 2024. This modest growth indicates a challenging environment where the construction sector lags the broader economy. While specialized segments like infrastructure show resilience, the overarching subdued sentiment, characterized by cautious investment and weakened confidence indicators, limits the potential for strong momentum and new project starts even for water, waste, and environmental engineering EPC firms.
forces.source_title: Europe's construction sector faces a period of weak growth

viewpoints.title: Europe's construction sector faces weak growth, with infrastructure as key support.
viewpoints.description: Europe's construction sector is expected to grow marginally by 0.5% in 2026, following declines in 2024. Despite overall subdued activity, infrastructure investment is identified as a crucial driver offsetting headwinds like higher financing costs and geopolitical risks. Specialised construction, including sustainability projects which encompass water and waste engineering, also contributes positively. This indicates that while the broader construction market is challenging, segments relevant to water, waste, and environmental engineering benefit from targeted investment, providing a cautious positive outlook for these specialized areas amidst general weakness.
viewpoints.source_title: Europe's construction sector faces a period of weak growth

viewpoints.title: Dutch infrastructure growth to slow significantly due to rising costs and constraints.
viewpoints.description: The Netherlands' infrastructure sector, a significant driver for water and waste engineering projects, is facing a deceleration in growth. After robust volume growth of 10.5% in 2025, a much lower growth rate is expected for 2026 and 2027. This slowdown is attributed to high construction costs, persistent staff shortages, nitrogen restrictions, and limited government budgets which prioritize maintenance over new construction. These factors will likely constrain new EPC contract opportunities in water and environmental engineering.

viewpoints.title: Irish construction strengthens, boosting civil engineering, despite cost and labor challenges.
viewpoints.description: Ireland's construction sector is experiencing a broad-based recovery, driven by sustained new order inflows, particularly in commercial and civil engineering. Civil engineering activity, relevant for water and waste infrastructure projects, is at its highest level since 2022. However, the sector still faces significant challenges including cost inflation, staff shortages, and lengthening delivery times. Companies in water, waste, and environmental engineering will benefit from increased project activity but must manage these operational and cost pressures diligently to maintain profitability and project timelines.

viewpoints.title: Norwegian construction activity low, but specialized infrastructure and rehabilitation offer some growth.
viewpoints.description: Overall construction activity in Norway remains low, with new-build projects (commercial and residential) being postponed due to high costs and interest rates. However, there's an expected pickup in activity for rehabilitation and maintenance, as both private and public entities prioritize upgrades. Government construction projects, energy supply development, and new data center buildouts are noted as lifting prospects, providing pockets of demand for water and waste engineering services, particularly for industrial or public infrastructure upgrades. Despite this, profitability in the sector generally remains weak.

demand_drivers.description: Supported by EU funds and spending on energy and digital networks, infrastructure projects provide an offset to weak building sector performance. This includes broader civil engineering which encompasses water and waste treatment plant EPC.

Benefits from renovation and sustainability projects, which can include upgrades to water treatment facilities, wastewater networks, or industrial waste management systems focused on environmental compliance.
